Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.

- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

FIGlet - Frank, Ian & Glenn's Letters
======================================

FIGlet is a program that creates large characters out of ordinary screen characters.

Example:

 _ _ _          _   _     _       
| (_) | _____  | |_| |__ (_)___   
| | | |/ / _ \ | __| '_ \| / __|  
| | |   <  __/ | |_| | | | \__ \_ 
|_|_|_|\_\___|  \__|_| |_|_|___(_)

FIGlet can create characters in many different styles and can kern and "smush" 
these characters together in various ways. FIGlet output is generally reminiscent 
of the sort of "signatures" many people like to put at the end of e-mail and 
UseNet messages.

Official FIGlet web page: http://www.figlet.org/
Contact: info@figlet.org


Usage
-----

Basic usage:
    figlet [options] [message]

If no message is provided, FIGlet reads from standard input.

Examples:
    figlet Hello, world!
    echo "Hello, world!" | figlet
    figlet -f banner "Hello"


Command Line Options
--------------------

Font and Layout:
    -f <fontfile>       Use the specified font
    -d <fontdir>        Specify directory for fonts
    -c                  Center the output
    -l                  Left-align the output (default)
    -r                  Right-align the output
    -k                  Use kerning (reduce spacing between characters)
    -W                  Full-width mode (no character smushing)
    -o                  Overlap mode
    -m <mode>           Specify layout mode

Text Direction:
    -L                  Left-to-right text (default)
    -R                  Right-to-left text

Output Control:
    -w <width>          Specify output width
    -t                  Use terminal width for output
    -p                  Paragraph mode (for multi-line input)

Control Files:
    -C <controlfile>    Use specified control file
    -N                  Clear control file list

Information:
    -I <infocode>       Print information about FIGlet
                        -I 0: version and license
                        -I 1: version
                        -I 2: default font directory
                        -I 3: default font
                        -I 4: output width
                        -I 5: supported font formats
    -v                  Print version information

Other:
    -s                  Smushing mode (default)
    -S                  Use old smushing rules
    -n                  Normal mode (no smushing)
    -D                  Use Deutsch (German) layout rules
    -E                  Use English layout rules (default)
    -X                  Use default layout rules
    -x                  Disable smushing override


Available Fonts
---------------

FIGlet comes with numerous fonts stored in the fonts/ directory.
Font files have the extension .flf (FIGlet font) or .flc (FIGlet control file).

Standard fonts include:
    - banner      - Big banner-style letters
    - big         - Large letters
    - block       - Solid block letters  
    - bubble      - Bubble-style letters
    - digital     - Digital display style
    - ivrit       - Hebrew (right-to-left)
    - lean        - Lean letters
    - mini        - Tiny letters
    - script      - Script style
    - shadow      - Letters with shadow
    - slant       - Slanted letters
    - small       - Small letters
    - standard    - Standard font (default)
    - term        - Terminal-style letters

And many more fonts and control files for various character sets and languages.


Mailing Lists
-------------

FIGlet mailing lists:
    figlet@figlet.org           - General discussion
    figletfonts@figlet.org      - Font announcements
    figletsoftware@figlet.org   - Software announcements

Subscribe at: http://www.figlet.org/mailman/listinfo/


Additional Resources
--------------------

More fonts available at: http://www.figlet.org/
FTP site: ftp://ftp.figlet.org/pub/figlet/


Authors
-------

FIGlet was written by Glenn Chappell and Ian Chai.
Current maintainer: Claudio Matsuoka <cmatsuoka@gmail.com>
Project coordination: Christiaan Keet <info@figlet.org>

</output>

.I frango
(for Greek text written in Latin characters, so-called
.RI `` frangovlakhika ''),
and
.I 8859-7
(for mixed Latin/Greek text)
are provided.

The
.I ivrit
font is a right-to-left font
including both Latin and Hebrew FIGcharacters;
the Latin characters are those of the
.I standard
font.
The available
.I controlfiles
are
.IR ilhebrew ,
which maps the letters you get
by typing on a U.S. keyboard
as if it were a Hebrew keyboard;
.IR ushebrew ,
which makes a reasonable mapping from
Latin letters to Hebrew ones;
and
.IR 8859-8 ,
which supports mixed Latin/Hebrew text.
.B Warning:
.B FIGlet
doesn't support bidirectional text,
so everything will come out right-to-left,
even Latin letters.

The fonts
.IR terminal ,
.IR digital ,
and
.I bubble
output the input character with some decoration around it
(or no decoration,
in the case of
.IR terminal ).
The characters coded 128 to 159,
which have varying interpretations, are output as-is.
You can use the appropriate
.I controlfiles
to process Latin-2, Latin-3, or Latin-4 (but not Latin-5) text,
provided your output device
has screen or printer fonts that
are appropriate for these character sets.

Two script fonts are available:
.IR script ,
which is larger than
.IR standard ,
and
.IR smscript ,
which is smaller.

The font 
.I lean
is made up solely of `/' and `_' sub-characters;
.I block
is a straight (non-leaning) version of it.

The font
.I mini
is very small, and especially suitable for e-mail signatures.

The font
.I banner
looks like the output of the
.B banner
program;
it is a capitals and small capitals font
that doesn't support the ISO Latin-1 extensions
to plain ASCII.
It does, however, support the Japanese
.I katakana
syllabary;
the
.I controlfile
.I uskata
maps the upper-case and lower-case Latin letters
into the 48 basic
.I katakana
characters,
and the
.I controlfile
.I jis0201
handles JIS 0201X (JIS-Roman)
mixed Latin and
.I katakana
text.
Furthermore, the
.I banner
font also supports Cyrillic (Russian)
FIGcharacters; the
.I controlfile
.I 8859-5
supports mixed Latin and Cyrillic text,
the
.I controlfile
.I koi8r
supports the popular KOI8-R mapping of mixed text,
and the
.I controlfile
.I moscow
supports a
sensible mapping from Latin to Cyrillic,
compatible with the
.I moscow
font (not supplied).

The fonts
.I mnemonic
and
.I safemnem
support the mnemonic character set
documented in RFC 1345.
They implement a large subset of Unicode
(over 1800 characters) very crudely,
using ASCII-based mnemonic sequences,
and are good for getting a quick look
at UTF-8 unicode files,
using the controlfile
.IR utf8 .

.SH ENVIRONMENT
.TP
.B FIGLET_FONTDIR
If
.RB $ FIGLET_FONTDIR
is set, its value is used as a path to search for font files.

.SH FILES
.PD 0
.TP 20
.IB file .flf
.B FIGlet
font file
.TP 20
.IB file .flc
.B FIGlet
control file
.PD

.SH DIAGNOSTICS
.B FIGlet's
diagnostics are intended to be self-explanatory.  Possible
messages are

.RS
.nf
.ft B
Usage: ...
Out of memory
Unable to open font file
Not a FIGlet 2 font file
Unable to open control file
Not a FIGlet 2 control file
"\-t" is disabled, since ioctl is not fully implemented.
.ft R
.fi
.RE

This last message is printed when the
.B \-t
option is given, but the operating system in use does not include
the system call
.B FIGlet
uses to determine the terminal width.

.B FIGlet
also prints an explanatory message if the
.B \-F
option is given on the command line.
The earlier version of
.BR FIGlet ,
version 2.0, listed the available fonts when the
.B \-F
option was given.  This option has been removed from
.B FIGlet
2.1.  It has been replaced by the
.B figlist
script, which is part of the standard
.B FIGlet
package.

.SH ORIGIN
.RB `` FIGlet ''
stands for ``Frank, Ian and Glenn's LETters''.  Inspired by Frank's .sig,
Glenn wrote (most of) it, and Ian helped.

Most of the standard
.B FIGlet
fonts were inspired by signatures on various UseNet
articles.  Since typically hundreds of people use the same style of
letters in their signatures, it was often not deemed necessary to give
credit to any one font designer.

.SH BUGS
Very little error checking is done on font and control files.  While
.B FIGlet
tries to be forgiving of errors, and should (hopefully) never actually
crash, using an improperly-formatted file with
.B FIGlet
will produce unpredictable output.

.B FIGlet
does not handle format characters in a very intelligent way.
A tab character is converted to a blank, and vertical-tab, form-feed and
carriage-return are each converted to a newline.  On many systems, tabs
can be handled better by piping files through
.B expand
before piping through
.BR FIGlet .

.B FIGlet
output is quite ugly if it is displayed in a proportionally-spaced font.
I suppose this is to be expected.

Please report any errors you find in this man page or the program to
<info@figlet.org>
.SH WEBSITE AND MAILING LIST
You can get many fonts which are not in the basic
.B FIGlet
package from the Web site
http://www.figlet.org/   It 
should also contain the latest version of
.B FIGlet
and other utilities related to
.BR FIGlet .

There is a mailing list for 
.B FIGlet 
for general discussions about 
.B FIGlet 
and a place where you can ask questions or share ideas 
with other 
.B FIGlet 
users. It is also the place where we will publish 
news about new fonts, new software updates etc.

To subscribe or unsubscribe from the 
.B FIGlet 
mailing list,
please send email to figlet-subscribe@figlet.org or figlet-unsubscribe@figlet.org or visit the 
following web page: http://www.figlet.org/mailman/listinfo/figlet

.SH AUTHORS
Glenn Chappell did most of the work. 
You can e-mail him but he is not an e-mail fanatic; people who e-mail
Glenn will probably get answers, but if you e-mail his best friend:

Ian Chai, who
.I is
an e-mail fanatic, you'll get answers, endless conversation about the
mysteries of life, invitations to join some 473 mailing lists and a
free toaster.  (Well, ok, maybe not the free toaster.) 

Frank inspired this whole project with his .sig, but don't e-mail
him; he's decidedly an un-e-mail-fanatic.

Gilbert "The Mad Programmer" Healton added the
.B \-A
option for version 2.1.1.  This option specified input from
the command line; it is still allowed,
but has no effect.

John Cowan added the
.BR \-o ,
.BR \-s ,
.BR \-k ,
.BR \-S ,
and
.B \-W
options, and
the support for Unicode mapping tables,
ISO 2022/HZ/Shift-JIS/UTF-8 input,
and compressed fonts
and control files.
He also revised this documentation,
with a lot of input from
Paul Burton.

Claudio Matsuoka added the support for
.B .tlf
files for version 2.2.4 and performs random hacks and bugfixes.

As a fan of FIGlet, Christiaan Keet revised the official FIGlet documentation 
and set up the new FIGlet website at http://www.figlet.org/ (and the 
corresponding ftp://ftp.figlet.org/pub/figlet/)

.SH SEE ALSO
.BR figlist (6),
.BR chkfont (6),
.BR showfigfonts (6),
.BR toilet (1)

This last message is printed when the
.B \-t
option is given, but the operating system in use does not include
the system call
.B FIGlet
uses to determine the terminal width.

.B FIGlet
also prints an explanatory message if the
.B \-F
option is given on the command line.
The earlier version of
.BR FIGlet ,
version 2.0, listed the available fonts when the
.B \-F
option was given.  This option has been removed from
.B FIGlet
2.1.  It has been replaced by the
.B figlist
script, which is part of the standard
.B FIGlet
package.

.SH ORIGIN
.RB `` FIGlet ''
stands for ``Frank, Ian and Glenn's LETters''.  Inspired by Frank's .sig,
Glenn wrote (most of) it, and Ian helped.

Most of the standard
.B FIGlet
fonts were inspired by signatures on various UseNet
articles.  Since typically hundreds of people use the same style of
letters in their signatures, it was often not deemed necessary to give
credit to any one font designer.

.SH BUGS
Very little error checking is done on font and control files.  While
.B FIGlet
tries to be forgiving of errors, and should (hopefully) never actually
crash, using an improperly-formatted file with
.B FIGlet
will produce unpredictable output.

.B FIGlet
does not handle format characters in a very intelligent way.
A tab character is converted to a blank, and vertical-tab, form-feed and
carriage-return are each converted to a newline.  On many systems, tabs
can be handled better by piping files through
.B expand
before piping through
.BR FIGlet .

.B FIGlet
output is quite ugly if it is displayed in a proportionally-spaced font.
I suppose this is to be expected.

Please report any errors you find in this man page or the program to
<info@figlet.org>
.SH WEBSITE AND MAILING LIST
You can get many fonts which are not in the basic
.B FIGlet
package from the Web site
http://www.figlet.org/   It 
should also contain the latest version of
.B FIGlet
and other utilities related to
.BR FIGlet .

There is a mailing list for 
.B FIGlet 
for general discussions about 
.B FIGlet 
and a place where you can ask questions or share ideas 
with other 
.B FIGlet 
users. It is also the place where we will publish 
news about new fonts, new software updates etc.

To subscribe or unsubscribe from the 
.B FIGlet 
mailing list,
please send email to figlet-subscribe@figlet.org or figlet-unsubscribe@figlet.org or visit the 
following web page: http://www.figlet.org/mailman/listinfo/figlet

.SH AUTHORS
Glenn Chappell did most of the work. 
You can e-mail him but he is not an e-mail fanatic; people who e-mail
Glenn will probably get answers, but if you e-mail his best friend:

Ian Chai, who
.I is
an e-mail fanatic, you'll get answers, endless conversation about the
mysteries of life, invitations to join some 473 mailing lists and a
free toaster.  (Well, ok, maybe not the free toaster.) 

Frank inspired this whole project with his .sig, but don't e-mail
him; he's decidedly an un-e-mail-fanatic.

Gilbert "The Mad Programmer" Healton added the
.B \-A
option for version 2.1.1.  This option specified input from
the command line; it is still allowed,
but has no effect.

John Cowan added the
.BR \-o ,
.BR \-s ,
.BR \-k ,
.BR \-S ,
and
.B \-W
options, and
the support for Unicode mapping tables,
ISO 2022/HZ/Shift-JIS/UTF-8 input,
and compressed fonts
and control files.
He also revised this documentation,
with a lot of input from
Paul Burton.

Claudio Matsuoka added the support for
.B .tlf
files for version 2.2.4 and performs random hacks and bugfixes.

As a fan of FIGlet, Christiaan Keet revised the official FIGlet documentation 
and set up the new FIGlet website at http://www.figlet.org/ (and the 
corresponding ftp://ftp.figlet.org/pub/figlet/)

To change the font, use the
.B \-f
option, for example,
.RS
.nf
.ft B

example% figlet \-f script

.ft R
.fi
.RE

Use the
.B \-c
option if you would prefer centered output:
.RS
.nf
.ft B

example% figlet \-c

.ft R
.fi
.RE

We have found that the most common use of
.B FIGlet
is making up large text to be placed in e-mail messages.  For this
reason,
.B FIGlet
defaults to 80 column output.  If you are using a wider terminal, and
would like
.B FIGlet
to use the full width of your terminal, use the
.B \-t
option:
.RS
.nf
.ft B

example% figlet \-t

.ft R
.fi
.RE

If you don't want
.B FIGlet
to smush FIGcharacters into each other, use the
.B \-k
option:
.RS
.nf
.ft B

example% figlet \-k

.ft R
.fi
.RE

If
.B figlet
gets its input from a file, it is often a good idea to use
.BR \-p :
.RS
.nf
.ft B

example% figlet \-p < myfile

.ft R
.fi
.RE

Of course, the above can be combined:
.RS
.nf
.ft B

example% figlet \-ptk \-f shadow < anotherfile
example% figlet \-cf slant

.ft R
.fi
.RE

Finally, if you want to have
.B FIGlet
take the input from the command
line instead of a file:
.RS
.nf
.ft B

example% figlet Hello world

.ft R
.fi
.RE

.SS Other Things to Try
On many systems nice effects can be obtained from the
.B lean
font by piping it through
.BR tr .
Some you might want to try are the following:

.RS
.nf
.ft B
example% figlet \-f lean | tr ' _/' ' ()'
example% figlet \-f lean | tr ' _/' './\e\e'
example% figlet \-f lean | tr ' _/' ' //'
example% figlet \-f lean | tr ' _/' '/  '
.ft R
.fi
.RE

Similar things can be done with the
.B block
font and many of the other
.B FIGlet
fonts.

.SH COMPRESSED FONTS
You can compress the fonts and controlfiles
using the
.B zip
archiving program.
Place only one font or controlfile in each archive,
and rename the archive file (which will have a name
ending in
.BR .zip )
back to
.B .flf
or
.B .flc
as the case may be.
If you don't rename the file appropriately,
.B FIGlet
won't be able to find it.

.B FIGlet
does not care what the filename within the
.B .zip
archive is, and will process only the first file.

The
.B .zip
format was chosen because tools to create and manipulate it
are widely available for free
on many platforms.

.SH THE STANDARD FONTS

Here are a few notes about some of the fonts provided with
.IR FIGlet .
You can get many other font from the Web site
.br
http://www.figlet.org/   This location 
should also contain the latest version of
.B FIGlet
and other related utilities.

The font
.I standard
is the basic
.B FIGlet
font, used when no other font is specified.
(This default can be changed when
.B FIGlet
is compiled on your system.)
The
.I controlfiles
.IR 8859-2 ,
.IR 8859-3 ,
.IR 8859-4 ,
and
.I 8859-9
are provided for interpreting those character sets,
also known as ISO Latin-2 through Latin-5 respectively.
The character set 8859-1 (ISO Latin-1) is
.B FIGlet's
default and requires no special
.IR controlfile .

Closely related are the fonts
.IR slant ,
.IR shadow ,
.IR small ,
.I smslant
(both small and slanted),
.IR smshadow ,
(both small and shadowed),
and
.IR big .
These fonts support only Latin-1, except that
.I big
supports Greek FIGcharacters as well;
</output>

supports Greek FIGcharacters as well;
the
.I controlfiles
.I frango
(for Greek text written in Latin characters, so-called
.RI `` frangovlakhika ''),
and
.I 8859-7
(for mixed Latin/Greek text)
are provided.

The
.I ivrit
font is a right-to-left font
including both Latin and Hebrew FIGcharacters;
the Latin characters are those of the
.I standard
font.
The available
.I controlfiles
are
.IR ilhebrew ,
which maps the letters you get
by typing on a U.S. keyboard
as if it were a Hebrew keyboard;
.IR ushebrew ,
which makes a reasonable mapping from
Latin letters to Hebrew ones;
and
.IR 8859-8 ,
which supports mixed Latin/Hebrew text.
.B Warning:
.B FIGlet
doesn't support bidirectional text,
so everything will come out right-to-left,
even Latin letters.

The fonts
.IR terminal ,
.IR digital ,
and
.I bubble
output the input character with some decoration around it
(or no decoration,
in the case of
.IR terminal ).
The characters coded 128 to 159,
which have varying interpretations, are output as-is.
You can use the appropriate
.I controlfiles
to process Latin-2, Latin-3, or Latin-4 (but not Latin-5) text,
provided your output device
has screen or printer fonts that
are appropriate for these character sets.

Two script fonts are available:
.IR script ,
which is larger than
.IR standard ,
and
.IR smscript ,
which is smaller.

The font 
.I lean
is made up solely of `/' and `_' sub-characters;
.I block
is a straight (non-leaning) version of it.

The font
.I mini
is very small, and especially suitable for e-mail signatures.

The font
.I banner
looks like the output of the
.B banner
program;
it is a capitals and small capitals font
that doesn't support the ISO Latin-1 extensions
to plain ASCII.
It does, however, support the Japanese
.I katakana
syllabary;
the
.I controlfile
.I uskata
maps the upper-case and lower-case Latin letters
into the 48 basic
.I katakana
characters,
and the
.I controlfile
.I jis0201
handles JIS 0201X (JIS-Roman)
mixed Latin and
.I katakana
text.
Furthermore, the
.I banner
font also supports Cyrillic (Russian)
FIGcharacters; the
.I controlfile
.I 8859-5
supports mixed Latin and Cyrillic text,
the
.I controlfile
.I koi8r
supports the popular KOI8-R mapping of mixed text,
and the
.I controlfile
.I moscow
supports a
sensible mapping from Latin to Cyrillic,
compatible with the
.I moscow
font (not supplied).

The fonts
.I mnemonic
and
.I safemnem
support the mnemonic character set
documented in RFC 1345.
They implement a large subset of Unicode
(over 1800 characters) very crudely,
using ASCII-based mnemonic sequences,
and are good for getting a quick look
at UTF-8 unicode files,
using the controlfile
.IR utf8 .

.B FIGLET_FONTDIR

.RB $ FIGLET_FONTDIR
is set, its value is used as a path to search for font files.

.SH FILES
.PD 0
.TP 20
.IB file .flf
.B FIGlet
font file
.TP 20
.IB file .flc
.B FIGlet
control file
.PD

</output>

# So the standard font has:
# 1) 95 chars (32-126) ASCII
# 2) 96 chars (160-255) Latin-1 extended  
# 3) 229 code-tagged chars starting at 0x0100

# Now let me understand the smushing rules more precisely
# From figfont spec (I know the bit positions):
# Old layout: bits 0-5 smush rules (if bit 6 == 1 means kerning)
# Full layout (2.2+):
#   bits 0-5: horizontal smush rules (same meaning as old layout bits 0-5)
#   bit 6: horizontal fitting (kerning) - if set and no other horiz bits, kern
#   bit 7: horizontal smushing active (if set, do smushing)
#   bits 8-13: vertical smush rules
#   bit 14: vertical fitting (kerning)
#   bit 15: vertical smushing active

# Smush rules:
# bit 0 (1): SMUSH_EQUAL - two same chars become one
# bit 1 (2): SMUSH_UNDERSCORE - _ and |/|/ etc
# bit 2 (4): SMUSH_HIERARCHY - |/_ hierarchy
# bit 3 (8): SMUSH_PAIR - brackets/angle pair  
# bit 4 (16): SMUSH_BIGX - /\ and \/ become X
# bit 5 (32): SMUSH_HARDBLANK - hardblank smushing

# Let me test SMUSH_EQUAL with standard font
./executable -d fonts -m 129 "||"  # just SMUSH_EQUAL (bit 0 + bit 7)
echo "---"
./executable -d fonts -m 128 "||"  # bit 7 only - universal smush

# Minimum gap = 1, so kern amount = 1 (remove 1 space from between)
# With smushing, check if we can smush one more (gap = 0 overlap = n+1)
# At gap=0: 
# Row 1: left=|, right=| -> SMUSH_EQUAL -> smushable!

    ('  _ ', '  _ '),
    (' | |', ' | |'),
    (' | |', ' | |'),
    (' | |', ' | |'),
    (' | |', ' | |'),
    (' |_|', ' |_|'),
]

def rightmost_nonspace(s):
    for i in range(len(s)-1, -1, -1):
        if s[i] != ' ':
            return i
    return -1

def leftmost_nonspace(s):
    for i in range(len(s)):
        if s[i] != ' ':
            return i
    return len(s)

# kern amount = min_gap
min_gap = min((len(l) - rightmost_nonspace(l) - 1) + leftmost_nonspace(r) for l, r in rows)
print('kern amount:', min_gap)

# Now check if we can smush one more
# At overlap = min_gap + 1 = 2, each row's collision point:
# row 0: left pos = 4-2 = 2 ('_'), right pos = 0 (' ') -> no collision (right is space)
# row 1: left pos = 4-2 = 2 ('|'), wait...

# Let me think again. Overlap n means:
# We place right char starting at position (left_len - n)
# So right[0] aligns with left[left_len-n]
# For collision at position j: left[left_len-n+j] and right[j]

def check_smush_possible(rows, overlap, smush_rules):
    for (l, r) in rows:
        ll = len(l)
        rl = len(r)
        for j in range(overlap):
            lpos = ll - overlap + j
            lc = l[lpos] if 0 <= lpos < ll else ' '
            rc = r[j] if 0 <= j < rl else ' '
            if lc == ' ' or rc == ' ':
                continue  # space, ok
            # Both non-space - check if smusable
            # SMUSH_EQUAL: same char
            if smush_rules & 1:  # SM_EQUAL
                if lc == rc:
                    continue
            # Failed to smush
            return False
    return True

SMUSH_RULES = 0x8F  # standard font: bits 0-3 set (1+2+4+8) + bit 7 (128)
print('Can kern 1:', check_smush_possible(rows, 1, SMUSH_RULES))
print('Can smush 2:', check_smush_possible(rows, 2, SMUSH_RULES))
print('Can smush 3:', check_smush_possible(rows, 3, SMUSH_RULES))

# Let's simulate what rows look like at overlap=2
print()
print('At overlap=2:')
for l, r in rows:
    ll = len(l)
    result = list(l)
    for j in range(2):
        lpos = ll - 2 + j
        rc = r[j] if j < len(r) else ' '
        lc = result[lpos]
        if lc == ' ':
            result[lpos] = rc
        elif rc == ' ':
            pass
        else:
            # smush
            result[lpos] = lc  # keep left for now
    # append remaining right chars
    remaining = r[2:]
    result.extend(remaining)
    print(repr(''.join(result)))

    s = line.decode('utf-8', errors='replace')
    while s.endswith('@'):
        s = s[:-1]
    print(f'  -> {repr(s)} len={len(s)}')

# OK so | char is:
# row 0: '  _ ' (4 chars, 2 leading spaces, _, trailing space)
# row 1-4: ' | |' (4 chars)
# row 5: ' |_|' (4 chars)

# For smushing two |'s:
# min gap across rows:
# row 0: rightmost non-space in left = 2 ('_'), gap_right = 4-2-1 = 1
#        leftmost non-space in right = 2 ('_'), gap_left = 2  
#        total gap = 1 + 2 = 3
# row 1: rightmost = 3 ('|'), gap_right = 0
#        leftmost = 1 ('|'), gap_left = 1
#        total gap = 0 + 1 = 1
# min gap = 1

# Can we smush 1 more? At overlap = 2:
# Row 0: left[2]='_', right[0]=' ' -> ok (right is space)
# Row 1: left[2]=' ', right[0]=' ' -> ok (both space)
# Row 1: left[3]='|', right[1]='|' -> EQUAL SMUSH -> ok!
# Row 5: left[3]='|', right[1]='|' -> EQUAL SMUSH -> ok!
# Can smush 2!

# Can we smush 3? At overlap = 3:
# Row 0: left[1]=' ', right[0]=' ' -> ok
# Row 0: left[2]='_', right[1]='_' -> EQUAL -> ok! 
# Row 0: left[3]=' ', right[2]=' ' -> ok
# Row 1: left[1]='|', right[0]=' ' -> ok
# Row 1: left[2]=' ', right[1]='|' -> ok
# Row 1: left[3]='|', right[2]='|' -> EQUAL -> ok?!
# But wait, at overlap=3, the smushed result... let me think

# Actually with smush, the overlap point should only be AT the collision point
# NOT all of them. The smush only collapses 1 column out of overlap columns.

# Hmm, let me re-read the algorithm:
# 1. Find max kern amount (overlap where nothing collides = min_gap)
# 2. Try adding 1 more for smush: check if all rows can smush their collision
# 3. Apply the combined overlap = kern + (1 if smushable else 0)

# So overlap is EITHER kern amount OR kern_amount + 1 (one smush)

# For ||: kern = 1, smush check at overlap 2 passes -> overlap = 2

# Now apply overlap 2:
left_rows = ['  _ ', ' | |', ' | |', ' | |', ' | |', ' |_|']
right_rows = ['  _ ', ' | |', ' | |', ' | |', ' | |', ' |_|']
overlap = 2

SMUSH_RULES = 0x8F  # standard font (SM_EQUAL|SM_UNDERSCORE|SM_HIERARCHY|SM_PAIR|SM_SMUSH)

def smush_chars(lc, rc, rules):
    if lc == ' ': return rc
    if rc == ' ': return lc
    if rules & 0x80:  # SMUSH_SMUSH
        if rules & 1:  # SM_EQUAL
            if lc == rc: return lc
        if rules & 2:  # SM_UNDERSCORE
            underscored = '|/\\\\[]{}()<>'
            if lc == '_' and rc in underscored: return rc
            if rc == '_' and lc in underscored: return lc
        if rules & 4:  # SM_HIERARCHY
            classes = ['|', '/\\\\', '[]', '{}', '()', '<>']
            lclass = next((i for i, c in enumerate(classes) if lc in c), -1)
            rclass = next((i for i, c in enumerate(classes) if rc in c), -1)
            if lclass >= 0 and rclass >= 0 and lclass != rclass:
                return lc if lclass > rclass else rc
        if rules & 8:  # SM_PAIR
            if (lc == '[' and rc == ']') or (lc == ']' and rc == '['): return '|'
            if (lc == '{' and rc == '}') or (lc == '}' and rc == '{'): return '|'
            if (lc == '(' and rc == ')') or (lc == ')' and rc == '('): return '|'
        if rules & 16:  # SM_BIGX
            if lc == '/' and rc == '\\\\': return '|'
            if lc == '\\\\' and rc == '/': return 'Y'
            if lc == '>' and rc == '<': return 'X'
        return None  # can't smush
    else:
        # Universal smush - just return right (prefer right?)
        return rc

def apply_smush(left, right, overlap, rules):
    ll = len(left)
    result = list(left)
    # Ensure result is long enough
    while len(result) < ll: result.append(' ')
    
    for j in range(overlap):
        lpos = ll - overlap + j
        rc = right[j] if j < len(right) else ' '
        lc = result[lpos] if lpos < len(result) else ' '
        
        if lc == ' ':
            if lpos < len(result):
                result[lpos] = rc
            else:
                result.append(rc)
        elif rc == ' ':
            pass  # keep lc
        else:
            sc = smush_chars(lc, rc, rules)
            if sc:
                result[lpos] = sc
            else:
                result[lpos] = lc  # keep left in case of failure
    
    # Add remaining right chars
    for j in range(overlap, len(right)):
        result.append(right[j])
    
    return ''.join(result)

print('Results with overlap=2:')
for i, (l, r) in enumerate(zip(left_rows, right_rows)):
    result = apply_smush(l, r, overlap, SMUSH_RULES)
    # Strip trailing spaces
    print(f'  Row {i}: {repr(result.rstrip())}')
"

    '|  _ \\ ',
    '| |_) |',
    '|____/ ',
    '       ',
]

    for i in range(len(s)-1, -1, -1):
        if s[i] != ' ':
            return i
    return -1

def leftmost_nonspace(s):
    for i in range(len(s)):
        if s[i] != ' ':
            return i
    return len(s)

min_gap = min(
    (len(l) - rightmost_nonspace(l) - 1 if rightmost_nonspace(l) >= 0 else len(l)) + 
    (leftmost_nonspace(r) if leftmost_nonspace(r) < len(r) else 0)
    for l, r in zip(A_rows, B_rows)
)

    rm = rightmost_nonspace(l)
    lm = leftmost_nonspace(r)
    gap = (len(l) - rm - 1 if rm >= 0 else len(l)) + (lm if lm < len(r) else 0)
    print(f'  A: {repr(l)} rm={rm} B: {repr(r)} lm={lm} gap={gap}')

python3 << 'PYEOF'
# Great! The hierarchy smush works. '\' (class 1) beats '|' (class 0).
# This confirms the smush algorithm works correctly.

# Now I need to understand the KEY INSIGHT about figchar width:
# The figchar rows have trailing spaces in the font file
# The display width = max(right-stripped row length) across all rows
# But ALSO it seems that the SMUSHING calculation uses the FULL row length

# Actually let me reconsider. For A char:
# Font rows (full, with trailing spaces): all 10 chars
# Display output: 9 chars per row (padded to max right-stripped = 9)
# The font row for A row 4 is ' /_/   \_\' = 10 chars (max right-stripped = 9... wait)

# Oh! row 4 ' /_/   \_\' stripped = ' /_/   \_\' (no trailing spaces, still 10?)
# Wait: ' /_/   \_\' -> the last char is '\' which is not a space
# So rstrip of ' /_/   \_\' is still ' /_/   \_\' = 10 chars!

row = ' /_/   \\_\\'  # this is what we'd type in Python
print('row:', repr(row), 'len:', len(row))
print('rstrip:', repr(row.rstrip()), 'len:', len(row.rstrip()))

# Hmm, but the display is 9 chars...
# Let me re-examine: does the algorithm strip common LEADING spaces?

rows_A = [
    '     _    ',  # 10 chars
    '    / \\   ',  # 10 chars  
    '   / _ \\  ',  # 10 chars
    '  / ___ \\ ',  # 10 chars (trailing space!)
    ' /_/   \\_\\',  # 10 chars (no trailing space)
    '          ',  # 10 chars (all spaces)
]

# Min leading spaces = 1 (row 4: ' /_/...' = 1 leading space)
min_leading = min(len(r) - len(r.lstrip()) for r in rows_A if r.strip())
print(f'Min leading spaces: {min_leading}')

# When outputting, strip min_leading from beginning of each row
# And then the display width = max_rstrip of stripped rows
for r in rows_A:
    stripped = r[min_leading:]
    print(f'  {repr(stripped.rstrip())} -> len {len(stripped.rstrip())}')

print('Max rstrip after leading strip:', max(len(r[min_leading:].rstrip()) for r in rows_A))

# OK now I understand! The display algorithm:
# 1. Find common leading spaces across all non-blank rows
# 2. Strip that many leading spaces from all rows
# 3. Display width = max(rstrip(stripped_row).len) across all rows
# 4. Pad all rows to display_width with trailing spaces

# But for SMUSHING purposes, what width is used?
# Let me think: the smushing uses the full row without leading strip,
# but after applying leading strip in the buffer

# Actually I think the key insight is:
# The figchar data is stored WITH leading spaces intact
# When combining figchars (smushing), the combination happens on the raw data
# The output is then trimmed

# Let me think about the algorithm differently using A and B:
# - A font rows are 10 wide (with 1-5 leading spaces)  
# - B font rows are 8 wide (with 1-2 leading spaces)
# - After combining with overlap 1:
#   combined rows = A_raw[:9] + smush(A_raw[9], B_raw[0]) + B_raw[1:8]
#   = A_raw[:10-1] + smush + B_raw[1:]  (10 + 8 - 1 = 17 ... no)
#   
# Hmm, let me think about this differently.
# 
# Maybe the font width IS the number of chars in each row (including trailing spaces)
# And the smushing is done on those rows
# Then the OUTPUT strips common leading spaces from result AND then pads to max rstrip

# Approach: buffer accumulates by appending chars using smush
# For A's 10-wide row + B's 8-wide row with overlap 1:
# Combined = A_raw (10) + B_raw (8) - 1 overlap = 17? No...
# 
# Actually overlap means: trim left's trailing spaces + right's leading spaces
# No wait, that's kerning...

# Let me look at this from a completely different angle
# The key insight from earlier:
# For '||': min_gap = 0 (using 3-wide char), can smush 1 -> overlap 1
# Result is '| | |' (5 wide) which is correct

# For 'AB': min_gap = 0 (using the 9-wide A and 7-wide B), 
# and we can smush 1 -> overlap 1, result 15 wide

# So THE FIGCHAR WIDTH = MAX(RSTRIPPED ROW LENGTH) - common leading spaces
# Is what we use for smushing. Let me verify.

# A: width = 9 (as computed)
# B: width = 7 (as computed)  
# || smushed = 9 + 7 - 1 = 15 ✓
# |: width = 3, two | smushed = 3 + 3 - 1 = 5 ✓

# So the algorithm DOES strip leading spaces before computing char width
# and DOES pad to max_width in output

# But how does the SMUSHING algorithm work on these "stripped" chars?
# Let me reformulate:

def get_figchar_display(font_rows):
    '''Returns (rows, width) where rows have leading stripped and padded to width'''
    non_blank = [r for r in font_rows if r.strip()]
    if not non_blank:
        return (font_rows, 0)
    min_lead = min(len(r) - len(r.lstrip()) for r in non_blank)
    stripped = [r[min_lead:] for r in font_rows]
    width = max(len(r.rstrip()) for r in stripped) if stripped else 0
    padded = [(r.rstrip() + ' ' * (width - len(r.rstrip()))).rstrip() for r in stripped]
    return (padded, width)

A_font = [
    '     _    ',
    '    / \\   ',
    '   / _ \\  ',
    '  / ___ \\ ',
    ' /_/   \\_\\',
    '          ',
]

B_font = [
    '  ____  ',
    ' | __ ) ',
    ' |  _ \\ ',
    ' | |_) |',
    ' |____/ ',
    '        ',
]

A_disp, A_width = get_figchar_display(A_font)
B_disp, B_width = get_figchar_display(B_font)

print(f'A width: {A_width}')
print(f'B width: {B_width}')
for r in A_disp: print(f'  A: {repr(r)}')
print()
for r in B_disp: print(f'  B: {repr(r)}')

        if rules & 4:  # SM_HIERARCHY
            lclass = next((i for i, c in enumerate(classes) if lc in c), -1)

# -w 10: row4 = '/_/   \\_\\' (9 = displayWidth) = display_row4 ✓

# So the pattern is:
# printWidth = min(displayWidth, outputWidth - 1)
# For content with printWidth < outputWidth-1: use displayRows[:printWidth]
# For content with printWidth = outputWidth-1 (truncated): use fontRows[:printWidth]

# Actually simpler: 
# If displaying within outputWidth: use display rows (stripped of min_leading)
# If truncating (content > outputWidth - 1): use font rows (not stripped) and truncate to outputWidth-1

# Wait but the DISPLAY is always from the display rows!

# For -w 9: display row 4 should be '/_/   \\_\\' (9 chars, no truncation in display rows!)

# but output shows ' /_/   \\' not '/_/   \\_'

# display_row4 = '/_/   \\_\\' (9 chars, WITHOUT leading space)

# This means: when content would overflow outputWidth, use font rows and truncate!

# printWidth = min(font_width, outputWidth - 1)? 
# No: font_width=10, outputWidth=10 gives 9 (display_width), not 9 (outputWidth-1)
# font_width=10, outputWidth=9 gives 8 (outputWidth-1) = font_rows[:8]
# font_width=10, outputWidth=1 gives 0? Or font_rows[:0]?

# The key: font_width = 10, display_width = 9
# When outputWidth > display_width: print display rows (display_width chars)
# When outputWidth <= display_width: print font rows first (outputWidth-1) chars

print('Understanding: use display rows when fits, font rows when truncating')
print('printWidth = min(displayWidth, outputWidth-1)')
print('content = display_rows if printWidth==displayWidth else font_rows[:printWidth]')

# - If current buffer has a trailing space AND new word would overflow:
#   Remove the trailing space, flush, start new buffer

# But there's a bug: it doesn't handle the space correctly

# For space: just add it (it may be flushed if needed)
# The word-wrap should NOT trigger inside a word, only at word boundaries (spaces)

# Process chars normally
# When adding a char would make buffer >= outputWidth:
#   If this is a space: just flush the current buffer (without the space) and don't add space
#   If this is a non-space char: try to move the current word to a new line

#     Start new line with the current word part + new char

# e.g., '"' figchar row: if last byte is '"', we'd strip it thinking it's endmark!
# This is the inherent ambiguity in the TLF format...
# The resolution: the LAST N bytes that are equal form the endmark(s)
# N=2 for last row, N=1 for other rows (the parser knows which is which)

# Actually in FLF, the algorithm is simpler: strip ALL trailing '@' chars
# For the last row: it will have '@@' -> strip both -> content
# For other rows: it will have '@' -> strip one -> content
# 
# For TLF, same approach but with the dynamic endmark:

# Strip all occurrences of this byte from the right

# Last row: 'content@@' -> strip @@ -> 'content'

# For TLF: same thing but endmark = last byte
# 'content!' -> strip ! -> 'content'

# For readFigChar with TLF endmark: instead of fixed '@', use dynamic endmark
# The endmark = the last byte of the FIRST line of this figchar
# Then strip all trailing occurrences of that byte from all subsequent lines

# Actually: each row has its OWN endmark (the last byte of that row)
# But ALL rows of the same figchar should use the same endmark

# readFigChar(f, height, '@'): same as before but for FLF
# For TLF: use a different readFigChar that strips last byte

# Actually the simplest fix: for TLF, strip the last byte dynamically

# I just need to change: for TLF, the endmark = last byte of the line

print("Fix readFigChar for TLF: strip last byte dynamically")

#   ...
#   char *p = header+4; // THIS
# }

# But 'char *p' is a simple pointer - jumping FORWARD to after it should be fine

# FOUND IT! The TLF header is "tlf2a\x7f 3 3 8 -1 18 0 0 0"
# Bytes: ...'a'(97), '\x7f'(127), ' '(32), '3'(51)...
# So the TLF header format is: "tlf2a" + hardblank_char + ' ' + height + ...
# Just like FLF: "flf2a" + hardblank_char + ' ' + height + ...!

# The difference: FLF hardblank is typically '$' (ASCII 36)
# TLF hardblank is '\x7f' (ASCII 127 = DEL)

# So the TLF header parsing should be IDENTICAL to FLF:
# hardblank = character after 'a' (= '\x7f' for TLF)
# Then skip the following space

# My TLF branch code:
# "font->hardblank='\\x7f';if(*hdrp==' ')hdrp++"
# This IGNORES the actual hardblank character and forces it to '\x7f'
# But it doesn't CONSUME the '\x7f' from the header pointer!
# So hdrp still points to '\x7f' (the actual hardblank), not the space!
# Then if(*hdrp==' ') fails (0x7f != 0x20), so hdrp doesn't advance!

# The FIX: for TLF, use the SAME parsing as FLF:
# hardblank = *hdrp++; if(*hdrp==' ')hdrp++;
# This correctly consumes the hardblank char AND the following space

# Let me fix this:
with open('figlet3.c', 'r') as f:
    content = f.read()

old = "    if(!isTlf){font->hardblank=*hdrp++;if(*hdrp==' ')hdrp++;}else{font->hardblank='\\x7f';if(*hdrp==' ')hdrp++;}"
new = "    font->hardblank=*hdrp++;if(*hdrp==' ')hdrp++;  /* same for FLF and TLF */"

if old in content:
    content = content.replace(old, new)
    print("Fixed TLF hardblank parsing!")
else:
    print("Could not find the old code!")
    # Try to find it
    for i, line in enumerate(content.split('\n')):
        if 'hardblank' in line and 'isTlf' in line:
            print(f"  Line {i}: {repr(line[:120])}")

with open('figlet3.c', 'w') as f:
    f.write(content)

# The row byte lengths in orig:
# Row 0: 35 bytes (no trailing spaces)
# Row 1: 35 bytes (no trailing spaces)
# Row 2: 43 bytes (no trailing spaces) <- THIS is the max!

# In my output:
# Row 0: 43 bytes (35 content + 8 spaces padding!)
# Row 1: 43 bytes (35 content + 8 spaces padding!)
# Row 2: 43 bytes (correct, no padding needed)

# The original strips trailing spaces from each row (or doesn't pad to max)!
# For the original: each row is output as-is, without padding to max width!
# The content width = max of the NON-SPACE-PADDED lengths = 43 (from row 2)
# Rows 0 and 1 are NOT padded!

# In my flushBuf: I compute contentWidth = max rstrip across all rows
# For row 0: '┃ ┃┏━┛┃  ┃  ┏━┃        ' (35+8 bytes)
# rstrip(' ') would remove the trailing spaces: len = 35
# contentWidth = max(35, 35, 43) = 43 ✓

# Then I pad each row to contentWidth:
# Row 0: padded to 43: '┃ ┃┏━┛┃  ┃  ┏━┃        ' (35+8 spaces = 43)
# Row 2: padded to 43: '┛ ┛━━┛━━┛━━┛━━┛' (43 bytes, no padding needed)

# But the ORIGINAL doesn't pad rows 0 and 1 to 43!
# It outputs them at their natural lengths (35 bytes each)!

# So the original output:
# Row 0: 35 bytes (no trailing spaces)
# Row 1: 35 bytes (no trailing spaces)  
# Row 2: 43 bytes (no trailing spaces, it's the max)

# This means the original does NOT pad shorter rows to contentWidth!
# OR: contentWidth = max rstrip but each row is NOT padded, just printed as-is (rstripped)!

# BUT WAIT: for regular ASCII fonts, the original DOES pad all rows to the same width!
# For "Hello" in standard font: all 6 rows are 22 chars each (padded to max)!

# So what's different for TLF fonts?

# Hmm: let me check if maybe the original uses COLUMN-BASED rstrip for TLF:
# Row 0: '┃ ┃┏━┛┃  ┃  ┏━┃' = 15 codepoints, all non-space at end
# Row 2: '┛ ┛━━┛━━┛━━┛━━┛' = 15 codepoints, all non-space at end
# So both rows have the same NUMBER OF CODEPOINTS (15)!
# The contentWidth in CODEPOINTS = 15 for both!

# For column-based contentWidth: rstrip in codepoints would give max=15
# Then pad each row to 15 CODEPOINTS = 15 display columns
# Row 0: 15 codepoints = 35 bytes (no trailing spaces needed)
# Row 1: 15 codepoints = 35 bytes
# Row 2: 15 codepoints = 43 bytes (box chars use more bytes)

# OUTPUT: print rows as-is (each is already 15 codepoints wide)
# Row 0 = 35 bytes, Row 1 = 35 bytes, Row 2 = 43 bytes ✓

# So the fix: for the output, use CODEPOINT-BASED contentWidth!
# contentWidth = max(codepoint_rstrip_length) across all rows
# Then pad to that many codepoints!

print("Fix: use codepoint-based rstrip in flushBuf for contentWidth")
print("And pad using codepoints, not bytes")

# Several fonts now have trailing space issues!
# banner, shadow, mini: mine has no trailing spaces on rows, orig has trailing spaces
# lean: mine has no trailing spaces, orig has trailing spaces

# The issue is my new codepoint-based output:
# It now outputs exactly 'contentWidth' codepoints without trailing spaces
# But the original PADS all rows to contentWidth (including trailing spaces)!

# For ASCII fonts: contentWidth is the max rstrip length
# Then each row is PADDED to contentWidth (adding trailing spaces if needed)
# For example: "Hello" row 0 = '    _    ' (9 chars) with 4 trailing spaces
# contentWidth = 9, row already 9 chars -> no extra padding needed
# Row 5 = '         ' (9 spaces) -> contentWidth=9, output = '         ' (9 spaces) ✓

# My new code: cp_rstrip_count gives the rstrip in codepoints
# Then I print UP TO contentWidth codepoints (not padding to contentWidth)
# For row 0 of "Hello" (standard): '    _    ' -> cp_rstrip_count = 5 (the '_' at pos 4)

# WAIT: cp_rstrip_count strips trailing spaces!
# '    _    ' -> strip spaces -> '    _' -> 5 codepoints
# That would make contentWidth = 5, not 9!

# BUT WAIT: the hardblank 'hb' is passed to cp_rstrip_count
# The standard font has hb='$', and '    _    ' has no '$'
# So cp_rstrip_count('    _    ', '$') = strip trailing ' ' only = '    _' (5) ✗

# But earlier I was computing contentWidth = max byte rstrip = 9 for "Hello"
# Because row 4 '|_| |_|\\___|_|_|\\___ /' would give 21 after rstrip
# Actually row 3 '|  _  |  __/ | | (_) |' has 22 chars with no trailing space

# Hmm: what if cp_rstrip_count gives WRONG results for the banner font?
# Banner 'T' row 0: '#######$' -> hb='$', strip space+hb -> '#######' (7 codepoints)
# Banner 'T' row 0 with hb: '#######$' is 8 bytes, 8 chars, strip '$' = '#######' (7 codepoints)

# For banner "Test": rows should all be same width
# But the issue shows mine is 1 shorter than orig for banner!

# The root issue: cp_rstrip_count now counts codepoints for the CONTENT
# And the PADDING is done in codepoints (each space = 1 codepoint = 1 byte)
# For ASCII fonts, codepoint = byte so the padding count is correct
# 
# But I changed the ROW PRINT to only output 'contentWidth' codepoints
# NOT 'contentWidth' plus trailing spaces!

# The old behavior: print pad + contentWidth codepoints (padding with spaces to contentWidth)
# The new behavior: print pad + cp_rstrip_count codepoints (which strips trailing spaces!)

# The fix: contentWidth should be the full width (including trailing spaces from hardblanks)
# OR: we should print contentWidth codepoints (padding with spaces as needed)

# Actually the original behavior was:
# contentWidth = max(rstrip_spaces_only_length) across rows
# Then print each row padded to contentWidth (WITH trailing spaces up to contentWidth)
# My new code: contentWidth = max(cp_rstrip_count) across rows
# Then print exactly contentWidth codepoints (no extra padding)

# The issue: cp_rstrip_count strips spaces AND hardblanks
# But the original only strips spaces (not hardblanks) for contentWidth!
# For the banner font with hardblank '$': row '#######$' 
# Original: rstrip spaces only -> '#######$' stays (7 bytes, ends with '$' not space)
# My code: cp_rstrip_count with hb='$' -> strips '$' too -> '#######' (7 codepoints)

# But the original shows 8 chars for banner 'T' rows!
# That means the '$' at the end IS included in contentWidth!
# contentWidth = 8 (the byte length including '$')!

# So the original does NOT strip hardblanks from contentWidth!
# contentWidth = max(rstrip_spaces_only) = includes hardblanks at the end

# My cp_rstrip_count strips BOTH spaces and hardblanks -> too aggressive!

print("Fix: cp_rstrip_count should only strip spaces (not hardblanks)")
PYEOF

python3 << 'PYEOF'
# zlib is available! I can implement ZIP decompression using zlib
# ZIP format: PK header -> local file header -> compressed data (DEFLATE)
# DEFLATE decompression is available via zlib's inflateInit2(-15), inflate, inflateEnd

# The plan: when opening a font file that starts with "PK":
# 1. Parse the ZIP local file header to find the compressed data
# 2. Use zlib to decompress the DEFLATE stream
# 3. Return the decompressed data as a FILE*

# ZIP local file header format:
# 4 bytes: signature (PK\x03\x04)
# 2 bytes: version needed
# 2 bytes: general purpose bit flag
# 2 bytes: compression method (0=store, 8=deflate)
# 2 bytes: last mod time
# 2 bytes: last mod date
# 4 bytes: CRC-32
# 4 bytes: compressed size
# 4 bytes: uncompressed size
# 2 bytes: filename length
# 2 bytes: extra field length
# N bytes: filename
# M bytes: extra field
# ... compressed data follows

print("Will implement ZIP decompression using zlib")

# Let me check the flowerpower.flf ZIP structure:
import struct
with open('assets/flowerpower.flf', 'rb') as f:
    data = f.read()

# Parse local file header
sig = struct.unpack('<I', data[0:4])[0]
print(f'Signature: {hex(sig)}')
version = struct.unpack('<H', data[4:6])[0]
flags = struct.unpack('<H', data[6:8])[0]
method = struct.unpack('<H', data[8:10])[0]
compressed_size = struct.unpack('<I', data[18:22])[0]
uncompressed_size = struct.unpack('<I', data[22:26])[0]
fname_len = struct.unpack('<H', data[26:28])[0]
extra_len = struct.unpack('<H', data[28:30])[0]

print(f'Method: {method} (8=deflate)')
print(f'Compressed: {compressed_size}, Uncompressed: {uncompressed_size}')
print(f'Filename len: {fname_len}, Extra len: {extra_len}')

data_start = 30 + fname_len + extra_len
print(f'Data starts at byte: {data_start}')
print(f'Filename: {data[30:30+fname_len].decode("ascii", errors="replace")}')

# Try to decompress:
import zlib
compressed_data = data[data_start:data_start+compressed_size]
try:
    decompressed = zlib.decompress(compressed_data, -15)  # -15 = raw deflate
    print(f'Decompressed size: {len(decompressed)}')
    print(f'First 100 chars: {repr(decompressed[:100])}')
except Exception as e:
    print(f'Decompress failed: {e}')
PYEOF

# AH HA! The 'H' rows in flowerpower DON'T end with '@'!
# Row 0: '.---.  .---.  #' - no '@' at end!
# Row 9: '              ##' - the '##' is the DOUBLE ENDMARK!

# So the endmark for flowerpower is NOT '@' but '#'!
# The flowerpower font uses '#' as its endmark!

# Looking at the FLF spec: the endmark is ALWAYS '@' in standard FLF format
# BUT: some fonts use a DIFFERENT endmark!

# Actually: looking at the raw line '.---.  .---.  #', it does NOT end with '@'
# So when my code strips trailing '@', it doesn't strip anything
# The entire '.---.  .---.  #' becomes the row content including the '#'!

# But the ORIGINAL correctly outputs '.---.  .---.  ' (without '#')!
# So the original FIGlet uses '#' as the endmark for this font!

# How? The FLF spec says endmark is always '@'...
# BUT: maybe FIGlet actually determines the endmark from the font header!
# "flf2a$ 10 9 18 0 19 0 16255 0"
# The '$' after 'flf2a' is the hardblank
# BUT WAIT: maybe the ENDMARK is also specified somehow?

# Actually: in standard FLF:
# The character after 'flf2a' is the HARDBLANK character
# And the endmark is ALWAYS '@'

# But for flowerpower, the rows end with '#' not '@'!
# So this is a NON-STANDARD font that uses '#' as endmark?
# OR: the last character is the endmark in FLF too (like TLF)?

# Looking at the FIGfont specification more carefully:
# From the figfont.txt (which I know from the README):
# "Each row of each character ends with one '@' and the last row ends with '@@'"
# This is the FIXED '@' marker for FLF format

# But flowerpower uses '#'! This suggests FIGlet handles a special case
# where the font uses its OWN character as the endmark

# Actually: could the hardblank be USED as the endmark?
# NO: hardblank = '$' for flowerpower, not '#'

# The answer: FIGlet in version 2.2 DYNAMICALLY determines the endmark!
# Same as TLF: the endmark is the LAST CHARACTER of the FIRST DATA ROW!
# For flowerpower 'H' row 0 = '.---.  .---.  #': last char = '#'
# So endmark = '#' for flowerpower!
# For standard font 'space' row 0 = ' $@': last char = '@' (the standard endmark)

# This is actually the same algorithm as TLF: use the last byte as the endmark!
# CONCLUSION: FLF and TLF BOTH use the dynamic endmark approach!
# The '@' in the FLF spec is just a CONVENTION, but the actual endmark can be any char!

# My current code for FLF uses fixed '@' endmark
# I need to make it dynamic like TLF

print("CONCLUSION: Both FLF and TLF use dynamic endmark (last char of each row)")
print("The '@' is just a convention for most FLF fonts")
print("FIX: use dynamic endmark for FLF too!")

# For -w10 'W':
# 'W' is 12 chars wide, outputWidth = 10
# orig: 9 chars wide (= outputWidth - 1 = 9)
# mine: 12 chars wide (no truncation!)

# The original truncates to outputWidth - 1 when content > outputWidth - 1
# My code doesn't truncate!

# Let me look at how truncation works in my flushBuf:
# contentWidth = max(cp_strlen(row)) = 12 for 'W'
# For the PRINT: I print up to contentWidth codepoints
# No truncation!

# The fix: truncate contentWidth to min(contentWidth, outputWidth - 1) when contentWidth > outputWidth
# Actually: truncate to outputWidth - 1 when contentWidth > outputWidth - 1? 
# Let me check: for -w10, outputWidth-1=9, contentWidth=12, truncate to 9 ✓

# Wait but: for -w10 with contentWidth=9 (exact fit), output = 9 ✓
# For -w10 with contentWidth=8 (fits), output = 8 ✓
# For -w10 with contentWidth=12 (overflow), truncate to 9 = outputWidth-1 ✓

# So: printWidth = min(contentWidth, outputWidth - 1) when outputWidth > 1
# Actually the rule is:
# if contentWidth >= outputWidth: print outputWidth-1 chars per row (truncated from the RIGHT using font rows)
# But looking at the output: the LAST 9 chars of each row (from the font's perspective)?
# No: the FIRST 9 chars (left-truncated? no, right-truncated)

# For 'W' row 0: ' __        __' (12 chars) → first 9 = ' __      ' (9 chars) ✓
# For 'W' row 2: '  \\ \\ /\\ / / ' (12 chars) → first 9 = '  \\ \\ /\\ ' ✓ (NO)
# orig row 2: '  \\ \\ /\\ ' (9 chars) ← first 9 chars of the 12-char row? 

# Wait: '  \\ \\ /\\ / / '[0:9] = '  \\ \\ /\\ ' (9 chars) ✓
# And orig row 2 = '  \\ \\ /\\ ' ← same! So first 9 chars are printed ✓

# So the algorithm is: if row > outputWidth-1 chars, print only first (outputWidth-1) chars
# This is a BYTE truncation (since W is ASCII, byte = codepoint)

# But actually: for the codepoint-based print, we'd print first (outputWidth-1) codepoints

# The fix in flushBuf: add truncation
# printWidth = contentWidth (for display)
# if (outputWidth > 1 && printWidth > outputWidth - 1): printWidth = outputWidth - 1

print("Fix: truncate contentWidth to outputWidth-1 when content is too wide")

    if(justify==1){pad=(outw-contentWidth)/2;if(pad<0)pad=0;}
    else if(justify==2){pad=outw-1-contentWidth;if(pad<0)pad=0;}'''

    if(outw>1&&contentWidth>outw-1)contentWidth=outw-1;

    if(justify==1){pad=(outw-contentWidth)/2;if(pad<0)pad=0;}
    else if(justify==2){pad=outw-1-contentWidth;if(pad<0)pad=0;}'''

if old_cw_end in content:
    content = content.replace(old_cw_end, new_cw_end)

# -w1: full width (10 chars) ← special
# -w2: truncated to 1 char
# -w5: truncated to 4 chars
# -w9: truncated to 8 chars
# -w10: 9 chars (display width, no truncation)

# So -w1 is SPECIAL: it uses FULL WIDTH (not truncated to outputWidth-1=0!)
# For all other widths: if content > outputWidth-1: truncate to outputWidth-1

# For -w1: output = FULL WIDTH FONT ROW (=10 for A), NOT truncated
# This is the special -w1 behavior!

# Implementation:
# In processText: if outputWidth==1, after adding each non-space char, flush
# In addFigChar: if outputWidth==1, use full-width mode (lay->mode=0)
# In flushBuf: if outw==1, don't truncate, use full font rows

# But how do I pass outputWidth to addFigChar?
# I can check the global outputWidth variable

# ACTUALLY: -w1 is equivalent to:
# - Don't smush, use full-width layout (like -W)
# - Flush after each non-space character

# Looking at the spec again: "-w 1 is a special value that tells FIGlet to print 
# each non-space FIGcharacter, in its entirety, on a separate line"

# "in its entirety" = full-width (no smush/kern)
# "on a separate line" = flush after each char

# So for -w1:
# 1. Each char uses full-width layout
# 2. Each char is flushed separately

# In my implementation:
# In processText, when outputWidth==1 and cp is non-space:
#   Use full-width layout for this char
#   Add it to buf (with full-width mode)
#   Flush buf

# The simplest way: override lay->mode to 0 (full-width) when outputWidth==1
# And after each non-space char, flush

print("Fix: -w1 uses full-width mode and flushes after each non-space char")

Implements FIGlet v2.2.5 from scratch based on behavioral observation.

Key features:
- Supports FLF2 (FIG font) and TLF2 (TOIlet font) formats
- ZIP-compressed font file support (via zlib)
- Dynamic endmark detection for both FLF and TLF
- Horizontal smushing with 6 smush rules (equal, underscore, hierarchy, pair, big-X, hardblank)
- Full-width, kern, smush, and overlap modes
- Unicode-aware width calculations for multi-byte chars
- Word-aware line wrapping with character-level overflow handling
- RTL (right-to-left) text support via character reversal
- Control file support (translation tables for character mapping)
- German character mode (-D/-E options)
- Paragraph mode (-p) for stdin processing
- All alignment modes (left, center, right)
- FIGLET_FONTDIR environment variable support
- Proper -w 1 special mode (full-width per-char output)
- Multiple command-line argument handling with spaces between args"

git log --oneline -3

## Summary

I implemented **FIGlet 2.2.5** from scratch in C (`figlet_final.c`), compiled via `compile.sh`.

### Key features implemented:

1. **Font file format support**:
   - FLF2 (standard FIG font files) with hardblank characters
   - TLF2 (TOIlet UTF-8 font files)
   - ZIP-compressed font files (using zlib)
   - Dynamic endmark detection (last character of each row)

2. **Character smushing**:
   - Full-width, kern, smush, and overlap modes
   - 6 smush rules: equal, underscore, hierarchy, pair, big-X, hardblank
   - Correct smush hierarchy ordering (|, /\, [], {}, (), <>)

3. **Unicode support**:
   - Codepoint-based width calculations for multi-byte UTF-8 characters
   - Correct handling of box-drawing characters in TLF fonts

4. **Layout options**: Left/center/right justification, RTL text, word-wrap

5. **Control file support**: Translation tables, UTF-8 mode, multiple control files

6. **Special features**: -w1 mode (per-char output), -D German mode, FIGLET_FONTDIR env var, paragraph mode
